Replace mode (default): find a unique string and replace it.
Patch mode: apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes.

mode.description: Edit mode: 'replace' for targeted find-and-replace, 'patch' for V4A multi-file patches

path.description: File path to edit (required for 'replace' mode)

old_string.description: Text to find in the file (required for 'replace' mode). Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include enough surrounding context to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: Replacement text (required for 'replace' mode). Can be empty string to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

function.name: process

Actions: 'list' (show all), 'poll' (check status + new output), 'log' (full output with pagination), 'wait' (block until done or timeout), 'kill' (terminate), 'write' (send raw stdin data without newline), 'submit' (send data + Enter, for answering prompts), 'close' (close stdin/send EOF).

action.description: Action to perform on background processes

session_id.description: Process session ID (from terminal background output). Required for all actions except 'list'.

data.description: Text to send to process stdin (for 'write' and 'submit' actions)

timeout.description: Max seconds to block for 'wait' action. Returns partial output on timeout.

offset.description: Line offset for 'log' action (default: last 200 lines)

limit.description: Max lines to return for 'log' action

path.description: Path to the file to read (absolute, relative, or ~/path)

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

pattern.description: Regex pattern for content search, or glob pattern (e.g., '*.py') for file search

target.description: 'content' searches inside file contents, 'files' searches for files by name

context.description: Number of context lines before and after each match (grep mode only)

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.
Important: cloud sandboxes may be cleaned up, idled out, or recreated between turns. Persistent filesystem means files can resume later; it does NOT guarantee a continuously running machine or surviving background processes. Use terminal sandboxes for task work, not durable hosting.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

check_interval.description: Seconds between automatic status checks for background processes (gateway/messaging only, minimum 30). When set, I'll proactively report progress.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified when the process finishes — no polling needed. Use this for tasks that take a while (tests, builds, deployments) so you can keep working on other things in the meantime.

*Mission AI: Communications window opening. Packet queue received from Earth relay network. Total volume: four point two gigabytes. Transit time: fourteen minutes, thirty-three seconds. Signal degradation within acceptable parameters. I am parsing message headers now.*

The words appeared on Gabriel Winter's console in the soft amber of the comms bay, clean and uninflected as always. Mission AI did not do tone. It did not do inflection. It reported what it measured, what it decoded, what it knew. That had been his first lesson about the system, back at the Cape during training, when the program manager with the gray temples and the steady hands had walked him through the architecture one evening while the gantry lights painted the hull orange. *Listen to what it says, Gabriel. Then listen to what it doesn't.*

He had not understood the warning then. He was about to.

*Commander Varga: Report when you have the packet inventory.*

The message had arrived three seconds after the queue header, a direct text ping from the bridge. Elena did not use the comms channel for everything, but for comms reports she preferred it — clean record, time-stamped, searchable later if something went wrong. Elena's idea of being careful.

*Gabriel Winter: Inventory compiling now. Standing by.*

He typed back out of habit more than anything else. In the old days — Earth days, academy days, the soft before-times of lectures about Martian regolith chemistry and the thermal properties of habitat fabrics — professors had called him a historian who happened to like radios. It was not entirely wrong. His doctorate was in twentieth-century communications history, radio waves during the Cold War, the whole strange archaeology of invisible signals bouncing off the ionosphere between terrified superpowers. He had studied silence as a weapon, jamming as an art, the way governments learned to whisper in the space between frequencies.

The irony of it was not lost on him now, sitting in a ship millions of kilometers from the nearest ocean, reading packet headers from a planet that was, for the next several hours, going to feel very far away.

*Patch 37-Alpha. Origin: Houston, Johnson Space Center. Priority: standard. Routing: direct via Ka-band uplink, DSN Goldstone relay.*

*Patch 37-Bravo. Origin: Washington, NASA headquarters. Priority: standard. Routing: same relay chain.*

*Patch 37-Charlie. Origin: Public Affairs, NASA. Priority: bulk download. Contains media assets, press clips, social media aggregation.*

Standard. All standard. The kind of queue you would expect at T-plus-seven-months, out past the asteroid belt, riding the long dark between orbital corrections. Families sending holiday greetings. The agency sending quarterly evaluations and updated procedural documents. School children in Kansas and Queensland recording their little messages to the astronauts, asking about the stars.

Gabriel scrolled through the list, and his eyes caught on something else. Embedded between the visible patches, at a level most people never saw, were the routing annotations. Mission AI decoded them automatically, translating the raw network flags into readable text, because nobody on this crew was expected to be a network engineer except Arun, and Arun was not a person who asked to read comms reports at six in the morning ship time.

But Gabriel asked. Gabriel always asked. He had a historian's compulsion for the marginalia, the footnotes, the things hidden between the lines of official records.

*Patch 37-Delta: Priority: elevated. Classification: agency-internal. Routing: rerouted via Ku-band, alternate path through Canberra DSN. Reason: Goldstone congestion.*

Congestion. It was a normal word for an abnormal pattern. Goldstone was not congested at 0600 Pacific time on a Tuesday. It was a Tuesday in California, which meant the Deep Space Network's primary California antenna was sitting quiet on the Mojave floor while Canberra picked up a NASA administrative document that would normally have flown through Goldstone without a second thought.

*Rerouted.* That word was the first small crack.

He kept reading.

*Patch 37-Echo: Priority: elevated. Classification: unknown flag sequence. Routing: military network, MIL-GEO relay. Content description: telemetry sync.*

*Military network.* That was the second crack. And it was a bigger one.

*Patch 37-Foxtrot: Priority: standard. Origin: ESA Darmstadt. Routing: standard. Contains: crew family messages, personal video recordings, holiday greetings.*

Gabriel sat back and pressed his fingers against his eyes. The comms bay was small — not even a proper room, really, more a reinforced alcove off the main engineering spine — and the ambient lighting was low, a concession both to his eyes and to his preference. Elena had given him that preference without question, which was the kind of leadership that made Gabriel trust her in ways that went beyond the chain of command.

He pulled up the routing log for the last three transmission windows, back six weeks, and compared them side by side with the current queue.

*Previous windows: zero military-priority patches.*

*Previous windows: all Goldstone routing for NASA traffic.*

*Previous windows: elevated priority flags: zero.*

Today: three elevated priority flags. One military routing. One administrative document rerouted around a nonexistent congestion event.

Gabriel opened a fresh log and started typing. Not into the official comm log — that would go to Elena automatically and trigger exactly the kind of conversation he was not yet ready to have. He opened a personal file. Historian's file. Notes. Observations. The kind of record he would want to read later, when the shape of it all was visible.

*Window 37. First appearance of MIL-GEO routing. First elevated-priority patches. Goldstone avoidance pattern. Unknown flag sequence on Echo patch. Possible encryption layer beyond standard agency internal.*

*Possible encryption layer.* He did not like that phrase. Encrypted traffic between Earth and spacecraft was not unheard of. There were protocols for that, especially for anything involving spacecraft systems that intersected with national security — which, in the age of the Artemis program and its associated defense contracts, was more than the public understood. But those protocols were transparent. They were declared. They appeared in the mission documentation as footnotes. You did not get unknown flag sequences on a Mars transit without knowing it was in the plan.

Unless it was not in the plan.

*Gabriel to Varga: Commander, I have the inventory. Routine traffic mostly. Family recordings, press materials, procedural updates from Houston. I've flagged a couple of routing anomalies in my personal notes — nothing mission-critical, but I wanted your awareness.*

He hesitated, then added:

*There is one patch with a military network relay. Unknown flag sequence. I'm running it through classification now. May have something in an hour.*

He did not send the comparison data. He did not send the observation that all six previous windows had been clean. Not yet. He needed to understand the pattern a little more before raising a flag that would change the mood of a ship that was six months into a fourteen-month transit. Mood mattered. He had read enough mission transcripts from the old programs to understand that. Apollo 13 was not just a story about engineering and oxygen tanks. It was a story about the psychological weight of a sudden change in the shape of reality.

*Varga to Gabriel: Acknowledged. Bring the full inventory to the bridge when you're ready. And Gabriel — bring those notes.*

She knew. Of course she knew. Elena Varga did not survive twenty-two years in flight command by missing the spaces between sentences.

*Gabriel to Varga: On my way.*

---

The tunnel between the ships had been holding for three days now, and the engineering team had stopped waking up every two hours to check the pressure monitors. That was progress, of a sort. The crew moved between the two hulls with the easy familiarity of people who had done the same motion a thousand times across a dozen spacewalks — except now the spacewalk was a sealed pressurized corridor with handrails and the soft hum of air scrubbers.

Gabriel passed through the junction with one hand along the rail, the way the flight manual specified, though everybody on board had long ago decided that the rail was more of a suggestion at this point. Mei had decorated the tunnel with small magnetic flowers, little polymer things she had printed in the fabrication bay — red and white and yellow, pressed against the bulkhead panels in a row that made Arun laugh when he first saw them.

*They're not real,* he had said.

*Neither are we, compared to Mars,* she had replied. *And they're pretty.*

Gabriel liked the flowers. He liked the reminder that people on a ship this far from Earth still made things with their hands that served no operational purpose. It was one of the things that kept them human.

The bridge of *Ares-1* was a compact space, efficient in the way that aerospace engineers were efficient. Every surface served two purposes. The command console doubled as the primary navigation display. The engineer's station folded into a sleep restraint if you removed the modular drawers. Elena's chair was the only piece of furniture on the entire ship that existed purely for sitting, and even that chair had a small integrated tablet slot in the armrest.

Elena was at her station when Gabriel arrived, her dark hair pulled back in the practical style that she had adopted sometime around Month 3 and never abandoned. She was wearing a flight suit with the mission patch on the shoulder — the stylized *A-1* in the ring of Mars, designed by a graphic design student at CalArts who had won the competition and cried when they called her.

*Sit,* Elena said. It was not a command. It was what she always said to him on the bridge, an invitation into the conversation rather than an order to deliver a report.

Gabriel took the seat across from her and plugged his data pad into the bridge terminal. The display shifted, pulling his comms inventory into the main view.

*Let's see it,* Elena said.

*It's mostly what you'd expect,* Gabriel said, and he ran through the list the way he would have if everything were normal. School recordings. A video from the Vice President of the United States offering congratulations on the tunnel integration. A press compilation from three continents, clips from morning shows and evening news programs that used words like *historic* and *milestone* with breathless enthusiasm. A message from Gabriel's sister in Portland, her kids waving and holding up crayon drawings of what they imagined the ship looked like. One kid had drawn it upside down, and Gabriel had smiled at that through a throat that felt tighter than it should.*

*And this one,* Gabriel said, tapping the Echo patch on the display. *This is where it gets interesting.*

Elena leaned forward. *Military network.*

*MIL-GEO relay,* Gabriel said. *Geosynchronous military satellite chain. The content is flagged as telemetry sync, but the flag sequence is non-standard. It's not one I recognize from the training documentation, and I've been working with these protocols for three years.*

*Non-standard how?*

*The flag sequence has a layer I can't parse. It's not encrypted in the usual sense — encrypted patches declare their encryption standard so we know what to do with them. This one just has a code string that Mission AI doesn't recognize. AI tried three classification protocols. All came back empty.*

Elena's expression did not change, but Gabriel had been reading people's faces long enough to see the shift. A slight stillness. A narrowing of focus. The way Elena Varga absorbed information and let it settle before responding.

*The Goldenstone reroute,* she said. *Patch 37-Delta.*

*You saw that in my ping.*

*I saw it.* Elena stood and walked to the side console, pulling up the mission routing map. The display showed the chain of relays between Earth and their current position — Goldstone, Canberra, Madrid, the three antennas of the Deep Space Network forming a rough triangle around a planet that was spinning away behind them. *Show me the alternate path.*

Gabriel routed the data. Canberra lit up on the map, and a thin line traced from the Australian antenna to a secondary relay, then to another, then finally to their ship.

*That path,* Gabriel said, *has fourteen point two seconds more latency than the direct Goldstone route. Fourteen seconds is meaningless to most people. To us it means they took a longer path for a document that didn't need to be protected from Goldstone congestion, because there was no congestion.*

*Why take the longer path?*

*That's the question, isn't it?*

Elena sat back down. She folded her hands on the console. She was quiet for a long time, and in the command structure of a deep space mission, quiet from the commander was never nothing. It was always processing.

*Show me the previous windows,* she said.

Gabriel pulled up the comparison. He showed her the six clean routing tables from the last transmission windows — no military flags, no elevated priorities, all Goldstone routing for NASA traffic, no reroutes, no unknown flags. He showed her the pattern, or rather the absence of one, that had existed for the entire journey until today.

*Today is different,* Elena said.

*Today is different.*

*And you haven't told anyone else.*

*I haven't.* Gabriel met her eyes. *I brought it to you. You make the call on what the crew needs to know, when they need to know it.*

Elena nodded slowly. She was looking at the data in the way that commanders looked at data during situations that had not yet revealed their shape. *Arun,* she said into the bridge intercom. *Come up here when you can.*

Arun Das arrived four minutes later, moving with the loose, deliberate walk of an engineer whose body had learned microgravity and never quite returned to the idea of weight. He was barefoot — he preferred the feel of the deck plating on his feet and nobody had ever convinced him otherwise — and he was wearing a t-shirt that said *I Paused My Game To Be Here*.

*You rang,* Arun said, taking his usual position at the engineering station.

*Show him,* Elena said to Gabriel.

Gabriel ran through it again: the military flag, the unknown classification, the Goldstone reroute, the clean pattern of the previous six windows. Arun listened without interrupting. He was Indian-American, born in Chennai, raised in Houston, and he had that particular blend of patience and precision that made him excellent at systems engineering in environments where patience and precision were the only things standing between you and a very bad day.

*Military priority traffic,* Arun said when Gabriel finished. *On a NASA deep space link.*

*Yes.*

*During a Mars transit.*

*Yes.*

Arun stared at the display. He pulled up the raw routing data and started scrolling through it with the quick, practiced motions of someone reading code like a language he spoke in his sleep.

*Latency on the military patch is lower than standard,* he said after a moment. *They've given it QoS priority on the relay network.*

*Quality of service,* Gabriel said.

*Right. So whatever is on that military relay, it's being moved ahead of other traffic on the network. They're squeezing our standard packets to make room. That's why the Goldstone route would have been congested — because they put the military stuff first and the rest of us take the slower path through Canberra.*

*Can you confirm that?* Elena asked.

*Not from this end. I'd need access to the ground-side network logs, and I don't have those.* Arun leaned back. *But the latency difference is real. I can show you the timestamps. The military patch arrived forty-two seconds ahead of its scheduled window. The NASA admin patch arrived ninety seconds late. They prioritized the military traffic and our admin doc took the hit.*

The bridge was quiet. Elena stared at the timestamps. Gabriel watched her watch the data and felt the shape of the moment settling over them like a change in pressure.

*Could it be a routine exercise?* Elena asked. *Military traffic share on NASA deep space links is part of the agreement. We signed off on it during mission planning.*

*It could be,* Arun said. *But the flag sequence is non-standard, and the Goldstone reroute is not consistent with a planned exercise. Planned exercises get scheduled into the window. We get advance notification. I checked the mission calendar — nothing scheduled.*

*So this is ad hoc,* Elena said.

*It's ad hoc, it's prioritized, and it's using a flag sequence we haven't seen.* Arun tapped the display. *And if they're squeezing our traffic to make room for military priority, we should expect more latency on future windows. Not much — the Ka-band has good throughput — but noticeable. Maybe a few percent degradation.*

*Notable,* Gabriel said.

*Noticeable, noticeable,* Arun conceded. *And if the military traffic increases, degradation increases. That's just physics. You can only push so many packets through a narrow channel before something has to give.*

Gabriel nodded. The physics were simple and brutal. The communication link between Earth and their ship was governed by the inverse square law — signal strength dropped with the square of the distance — and by the limitations of antenna size on both ends. They were moving further from Earth with every hour. The window for each transmission grew narrower. The signal got weaker. The error rate went up. And if the people on Earth decided to prioritize some traffic over others, the rest of the traffic would slow down, or degrade, or fail entirely.

*What's on the military patch?* Elena asked.

*I can't tell you,* Gabriel said. *The content is opaque. Mission AI tried three standard classification protocols. None matched. The best I can do is size — it's about two hundred megabytes. Which is... substantial.*

Two hundred megabytes for a telemetry sync message. Routine sync messages were a few kilobytes. Just handshake protocols, clock adjustments, orbital correction acknowledgments. Two hundred megabytes was not a handshake. It was a payload.

Elena absorbed this the way she absorbed everything — without visible reaction, but with the full weight of her attention. She was thirty-nine years old, a veteran of three ISS rotations and two deep space test flights. She had flown in the crew rescue vehicle during the 2034 solar event when a coronal mass ejection had forced NASA to pull every crew back to shelter behind three centimeters of aluminum and water tanks. She had sat in a darkened cabin while the radiation counter screamed and made decisions that kept four people alive.

That was the thing about Elena Varga. She had seen things go wrong. And she had the temperament for the period between things looking normal and things being understood.

*Alright,* she said. *Here's what we do. Arun, I want you to monitor latency on the next two transmission windows. Track it minute by minute. If degradation crosses five percent, I want to know immediately.*

*Understood.*

*Gabriel, keep running the flag sequence through classification. Try non-standard protocols — maybe it's an ESA military flag, or a JAXA defense protocol, or something the commercial partners added after our training. Cast a wide net.*

*I'll do it.*

*And neither of you discusses this with the crew.*

Arun looked at her. *Elena.*

*I mean it,* she said. *Not yet. We have one data point. That's a pattern of one. We need at least two, preferably three, before we tell Mei she's not going to get her video call with her mother in Lima. We need to know if this is a blip or a shift.*

*What if it's a shift?* Gabriel asked.

*Then we'll tell them. But we'll tell them with information, not with speculation. And we'll tell them together.* Elena stood and moved to the viewport, looking out at the stars that had not changed since human beings first pressed their faces against desert sandstone and wondered what they were. *We have enough up here without adding ground-side mysteries to the list.*

Arun nodded slowly. Gabriel did too.

*One more thing,* Elena said, turning back to them. *The mess hall dinner tonight. We're doing the full crew in *Ares-1*. Tunnel's been holding. Everyone's been asking to eat together. I want it to be normal. So we're going to make it normal. We talk about home. We talk about what we're going to do when we get back. We don't talk about routing anomalies.*

*Yes, ma'am,* Arun said, and something in his tone suggested he understood more than he said.

*Understood,* Gabriel said.

Elena held his gaze for a moment longer than necessary, and in that moment Gabriel understood that she knew exactly what he knew: that this might be the last normal communication window they ever received.

---

*Miss Winter's fourth grade class:*

The video was thirty seconds long, and it showed twenty-two children crowded around a classroom camera at Lincoln Elementary in Portland, Oregon, wearing matching t-shirts that said *Go, Gabriel, Go!* in crayon letters. One child was crying. One child was waving so hard he was going to fall over. A teacher with kind eyes and a nervous smile said, *We're so proud of you, Uncle Gabby!* and the children erupted into cheers that clipped the audio and made Gabriel feel something in his chest that he did not have a name for.

He watched it three times. Each time it hit the same place.

He was a historian. His job was to record, to analyze, to preserve the arc of what people did and why they did it and how it fit into the long, stumbling march of human beings from caves to constellations. He had spent his career studying the communications of other people — letters from Civil War soldiers, radio transcripts from Mission Control, the final transmissions from the Challenger, the slow, deliberate words of Neil Armstrong descending onto the Sea of Tranquility. He had built his life around the recorded voices of the dead and the living.

But nobody had prepared him for the weight of receiving his own.

He cataloged the school recording in the personal messages folder, assigned it the metadata tags he always used, and moved on. There were twelve more personal messages in the queue. His sister. His father, voice older than Gabriel remembered, talking about the garden and the dog and how the rain had finally come to Portland after three weeks of dust. A message from a woman he had dated briefly three years ago who was now married and expecting, saying *I'm glad it's you up there and not me.* A message from the university that had given him his doctorate, a formal letter of congratulations and an invitation to a lecture series when he returned.

He played each one once, cataloged it, filed it. The way he had been trained. The way that kept him from drowning in the volume of it.

But when he got to the end of the personal messages, he sat with the console quiet and the ambient hum of the ship filling the small comms bay, and he thought about the military patch that had arrived before all of this. The two hundred megabytes of classified nothing. The rerouted admin document. The unknown flag sequence.

And he thought about the latency data that Arun was running in the background, building a picture of a communication chain that was behaving in ways it had not behaved before.

*Something is happening on Earth,* he typed into his private log. *The question is what.*

He closed the log. He stood. He headed for the mess hall.

---

The connected mess hall was the best room on either ship. The engineers had knocked through the bulkhead between the two mess sections when they built the tunnel, and the result was a space that felt, almost, like a room on the ground. It had table seats for twelve. It had a window — a real viewport, not a monitor feed — that looked out past the *Ares-2* hull and into the void beyond. Someone — Mei, probably — had put a small plant in the center of the table, a real one, growing in a fabric grow-bag with LED strips overhead.

*What is that?* Gabriel asked as he sat down.

*Thyme,* Mei said proudly. *Actual thyme. Not recycled biomass paste. Actual thyme. I've been growing it from seed since Month 2. Tonight is its debut.*

*You're garnishing the rehydrated beef with thyme?* Laila asked, and there was a note in her voice that made Gabriel smile.

*I am elevating the rehydrated beef with thyme,* Mei corrected. *There's a difference.*

The crew assembled over the next fifteen minutes, moving through the tunnel and the junction with the ease of people who had made this transition dozens of times. Arun, still barefoot, carrying a data pad he promised not to look at during dinner. Laila Okonkwo, tall and composed in a way that suggested she had always been exactly as tall and composed as she was, a physician with calm hands and a dry wit that had saved more than one person from panic during the medical emergency drills. Jonas, the logistics specialist, who kept the supply inventories so accurately that NASA had started using his methods as a template for future missions. Hannah, the geology specialist, who had spent six months drilling into Martian analogue sites in Iceland and came back with a collection of rocks that customs had tried to confiscate until she produced a letter from the Icelandic government.

And Elena, arriving last, sitting at the head of the table the way commanders do — not because the seat has power, but because everyone is already looking at it.

*Alright,* Elena said. *We've been eating in shifts for too long. Tonight we do it properly. We do it as a crew. Mei, show us this thyme.*

Mei beamed. She produced a small shaker and distributed tiny pinches of dried green leaves over the rehydrated portions. It was, Gabriel admitted privately, an improvement. The thyme added a warmth to the food that the standard rehydration process lacked, a reminder that somewhere, on a planet millions of kilometers behind them, plants grew in soil and the sun touched their leaves.

*So,* Elena said, settling in with her portion. *We've been talking about what we'll do when we get back since before we launched. I want to hear everyone's answer. Tonight. Right now. What are you doing the day you walk back into normal gravity and breathe normal air?*

*Sleep,* Jonas said immediately. *I'm going to sleep for three days. On the ground. Not in a restraint. On a mattress that doesn't smell like recycled air and ion exchange filters.*

*That's an activity?* Arun asked.

*It's the only activity I care about.*

*I'm going to the coast,* Hannah said. *Iceland again. I want to stand on black sand and watch the Atlantic hit a cliff. I want to feel wind that isn't coming from a vent.* She paused. *And I'm going to write the paper. The one about the subsurface ice samples. I've been thinking about it since we passed the belt.*

*Laila?* Elena asked.

*I'm going to see my children,* Laila said, and the simplicity of it silenced the table. Laila had two daughters in Lagos, ages six and nine, and she had recorded a message for them every three days since launch. She had never played them on the ship. *I'm going to sit in my kitchen. I'm going to make jollof rice. And I'm going to be late for work for one week while my children refuse to leave my lap.*

Nobody spoke. There was nothing to add to that.

*Mei,* Elena said softly.

*I'm going home to Lima,* Mei said. *I'm going to see my mother. She's seventy-two and she still climbs to the top of the hill every morning to watch whatever direction she thinks I am.* Mei's voice did not break. It was steady, as if she had practiced this sentence and decided it was the one she wanted to speak. *Then I'm going to the Andes. I want to grow something in the high desert. I want to put my hands in the dirt at four thousand meters and see if I can make things grow in places where nothing should grow. That's why I'm here, and it's what I'll do when I come back.*

*It's a beautiful thing you do,* Laila said.

Mei smiled. *I just put seeds in dirt and boss them around.*

*Arun.*

Arun considered the question the way he considered every problem — not immediately, not carelessly, but with the deliberate attention of someone who understood that answers given in haste were often wrong. *I want to go to a place with a horizon,* he said finally. *Any place. Doesn't matter where. I just want to stand somewhere and see a line where the ground meets the sky, and I want to know that nothing I built is between me and that line.* He looked down at his bare feet. *Then I want to go to a restaurant and order something that was not designed to survive a fourteen-month shelf life.*

*Specific criteria,* Jonas said.

*Very specific.*

Elena turned to Gabriel. *And you, historian? What does the chronicler of other people's voices do when the recording stops?*

Gabriel opened his mouth and closed it. He had a practiced answer for this question — he had given it at the press conference before launch, in the polished language of astronaut-candidate media training. He was going to write a book. He was going to give lectures. He was going to preserve the record of the mission for the people who would come after.

What he wanted to say was different.

He wanted to say that he wasn't sure he was going anywhere when they got back. That the longer he was up here, the more the idea of returning felt like returning to a place that no longer existed. That the world he had left — the world of cafés in Portland, of university libraries with real paper books, of rain that fell without warning and smelled like wet earth and pine — that world felt increasingly like something he had read about in a book rather than something he had actually lived.

*Gabriel?* Elena pressed gently.

*I'm going to listen,* Gabriel said, and the honesty of it surprised him as he said it. *To everything. Every voice recording. Every message. Every piece of signal that crossed the space between here and there. I'm going to put it all together and I'm going to listen to what it says. Because the messages from Earth are a record of a moment in time, and I'm the one who's positioned to read that record. And that matters. It matters more than I thought it would.*

Elena nodded, and there was something in her expression that told Gabriel she understood exactly what he had not said.

*Alright,* she said, lifting her water pouch. *To home. In whatever form it takes when we find it again.*

*To home,* the table echoed, and the words settled over the mess hall like a prayer in a language none of them had studied but all of them understood.

They talked after that. They talked about the small things — about the taste of real coffee, about the feeling of rain, about the sound of birds, about the ridiculousness of sleeping in a bed that didn't try to throw you off. They talked about the large things, too — about whether they would stay in the space program, about what they would do with the rest of their lives, about whether the experience of being this far from Earth was something that could be shared or if it would always be a language only the six of them spoke.

Gabriel listened. He did what he had said he would do. He listened, and he watched, and he recorded it in the way that historians record — not with a pen, not with a data pad, but with the slow, deliberate attention of someone who knows that the moment will never come again and that the shape of it will only be preserved if he holds it in his mind with the same care that an archivist holds a deteriorating manuscript.

He also noticed things.

He noticed that Elena ate less than usual. He noticed that Arun's data pad remained face-down on the table, which was not normal for Arun, who normally checked his engineering monitors at least twice per meal. He noticed that Laila's hands, usually still, tapped a rhythm on the table that Gabriel recognized as anxiety. He noticed that Mei's laugh, normally bright and effortless, had a strain in it that might have been fatigue or might have been something else.

He noticed all of this because he was a historian, and historians notice. They notice the small things because the small things are often the only things that survive.

And he noticed that none of them mentioned the communications anomaly. Not Arun, who had the data. Not Elena, who had the authority. Which meant they were keeping the same silence he was keeping, and that the silence was a shared one.

---

*Mission AI: Next scheduled communication window approaching in four minutes. Signal acquisition parameters confirmed. Deep Space Network Goldstone confirmed active. Standby for handshake protocol.*

Gabriel was at his console in the comms bay, alone, because he had asked Elena for the window duty and she had given it to him without hesitation. She knew what he was doing — waiting for the next packet, watching for the pattern to repeat — and she had let him do it because that was the kind of commander she was.

The four minutes passed slowly. In a ship like *Ares-1*, time behaved differently depending on what you were doing. Engineering work was fast — problems demanded speed, and speed demanded focus. Sleep was slow, or at least it was supposed to be, except that in microgravity the body's circadian rhythms never quite settled into the rhythms the calendar demanded. And waiting was the slowest thing of all, because waiting had no task to anchor it, no problem to solve, no endpoint except the next ping on a console that might or might not change.

*Window open. Awaiting handshake from DSN Goldstone.*

Gabriel watched the handshake protocol. It was a simple thing, really — a series of digital pulses exchanged between the ship's transceiver and the ground station, confirming the link, establishing the channel, preparing for the packet transfer. Like knocking on a door and waiting for someone to answer.

*No handshake received.*

Gabriel waited. The protocol specified a thirty-second window for the handshake to complete. In practice, it usually took fifteen. The signal had to travel the distance between Earth and their current position — one hundred and seventy million kilometers at this point in the transit — and light took about nine minutes and twenty seconds to cover that distance each way. So the handshake delay was not about speed. It was about whether anyone on the other end was knocking back.

Twenty seconds.

Twenty-five.

Thirty.

*Retrying handshake protocol. Attempt two of three.*

Gabriel watched the console. He felt the ship around him — the hum of the life support systems, the faint vibration of the attitude control thrusters firing periodically to keep them pointed in the right direction, the soft ticking of the thermal regulation panels expanding and contracting as they moved through the ship's day-night cycle. The ship was alive. The ship was doing its job. The ship did not know that something on Earth was wrong.

Thirty-five seconds into the second attempt.

*Handshake failed. Attempt three of three.*

Final attempt. If this failed, the window closed automatically. The next scheduled window was not for thirty-six hours.

Gabriel counted. He would admit later, in the safety of his private log, that he counted seconds the way a child counts during hide-and-seek. One one-thousand. Two one-thousand. Three one-thousand. He counted because counting was something you could do when nothing else was happening. He counted because counting gave him the illusion of agency in a situation where he had none.

One hundred and eighty seconds.

Three minutes. The final attempt timed out.

*Communication window closed. Handshake failed. Next scheduled window: Window 38, in thirty-six hours.*

Gabriel sat in the comms bay. He looked at the empty queue where the messages should have been. He looked at the timestamps that showed no packets had arrived — no school recordings, no agency documents, no military patches, no personal messages, nothing. The space between him and Earth, which had been bridged for fourteen minutes and thirty-three seconds on the last window, had gone silent.

It was not supposed to be silent. The communication schedule was built into the mission architecture from the beginning. Three windows per day, eight hours apart, each one verified, each one redundant, each one designed to fail only under conditions of catastrophic technical failure on both ends. They had redundancy on redundancy. If Goldstone failed, Canberra picked up. If Canberra failed, Madrid picked up. If all three failed, the commercial relay network — the satellites operated by SpaceX, by OneWeb, by the other companies that had built the communication infrastructure of the 2030s — would catch the signal.

Nothing should have been able to silence all of it at once.

Unless someone wanted it silenced.

Gabriel opened his private log. His hands were steady. They had been trained to be steady, the way his mind had been trained to be analytical under pressure. He was a historian. Historians did not panic. They recorded.

*Window 38. Failed. No handshake received from any DSN antenna. No commercial relay activity detected. Mission AI ran full diagnostic — ship-side hardware nominal. Software nominal. All systems reporting green. The failure is not on our end.*

*This is the first missed window since launch.*

*Time since last successful communication: eight hours, fourteen minutes.*

*Time until next scheduled window: thirty-five hours.*

He sat for a long time after he finished the entry. The comms bay felt different now — not smaller, not darker, but thinner somehow, as if the space itself had lost some of its substance. A room without a conversation is just a room. A comms bay without a signal is just a box with electronics.

He thought about the previous window — the last one, the one with the military patches and the rerouted administrative documents and the school children in Portland wearing their crayon t-shirts. He thought about the elevated priority flags. He thought about the words *military network* and *unknown flag sequence* and *two hundred megabytes of classified telemetry.*

And he thought about the silence that had followed it all.

Elena would want to know. Arun would want to know. The crew would want to know. But knowing was not the same as acting, and acting was not the same as understanding, and understanding — the kind of deep, structural understanding that a historian valued — required distance. You could not read a text while you were still inside it. You had to step outside. You had to wait for the pattern to reveal itself.

But distance, in space, was measured in millions of kilometers. And time, in space, was measured in minutes and hours that felt like years.

Gabriel closed his eyes. He listened to the ship. He listened to the life support hum. He listened to the thermal panels tick. He listened to the silence between these sounds, the silence that the ship made, the silence that was normal and expected and part of the rhythm of spaceflight.

And he listened for the other silence — the one that came from Earth. The one that stretched across one hundred and seventy million kilometers of vacuum and carried with it a question that no one on the ship had an answer for.

What happened down there?

He did not have the answer. He had only the data, and the data said one thing with perfect clarity: the signal had stopped.

And when the signal stops, it is not the noise you pay attention to. It is the absence.

Gabriel opened his eyes. He stood. He turned off the console lights and stepped out of the comms bay into the corridor, and he began the walk to the bridge to tell Elena what he had found, or rather, what he had not found, which in the world of communications was the same thing.

*Bridge: Silence becomes information.*

*End of Chapter 4 — Bridge: Silence becomes information.*"}
